voiceover.text: Last time, column three: the conditions that aren't yours to change. So take the condition you'd escalate, and answer the question that decides whether anything happens. Who, by name or by role, has the power to change it? Not the government. A person, a position, a committee or a council. If you can't name one, finding out is your first job, not a reason to stop.

That's advocacy: speaking or acting to change the conditions, decisions or policies that affect health, your own or other people's. Every personal skill so far works on what a person does. Advocacy works on what they're doing it within, and it's how young people push for the regulation, services and environments you met earlier. So it isn't health education, which teaches someone something. It isn't awareness-raising, which makes an issue visible but asks nobody to act. And it isn't personal behaviour change, which aims at column one. It also runs two ways. Self-advocacy is acting for your own health, like asking a doctor for a referral. Advocacy for others acts for people who can't easily act for themselves.

Every piece of advocacy needs two things: an ask, the one specific thing you want done, and an audience, the decision-maker who can grant it. Raise awareness of youth mental health fails both. Ask the council to run the last bus past the youth health centre until seven pm, not five, passes both, and it's small enough to win. A specific ask aimed at the body that can say yes beats a big campaign aimed at nobody.

To examine a campaign, the syllabus says use various sources, and various means different kinds, not three news articles. Each kind fails in its own way. News covers the launch, and rarely says whether anything changed a year later. Campaign material states the ask, but reports its own success. Government reports are detailed, but slow. And social media shows reach, but engagement isn't impact. So ask four questions of every source. Who made it, and what did they want? When, and has anything happened since? Is it claiming something happened, or that something worked? And what would disagree with it?

Here's a past example. In nineteen sixty-five, a group of university students, Aboriginal students among them, toured country towns in New South Wales by bus to expose the segregation of Aboriginal people. It belongs in a health course because of what it targeted: being barred from swimming pools, refused service, and poor living conditions on the edges of towns. Those are determinants of health. Four features generalise. They made a hidden condition visible, by bringing journalists. Their ask was local and specific, like entry to one town's pool. They acted with and for others, which raises the question of who leads. And the effect was delayed: national attention first, then longer change.

scenes.title: current advocacy: what changed, what didn't

voiceover.text: Now, current advocacy. Young Australians campaign on mental health services and waiting times, vaping, consent education, climate as a health issue, and access to sport. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people advocate through community-controlled organisations, for services designed by community, not just for it. Three things have changed since nineteen sixty-five. Reaching an audience costs almost nothing. Testimony can be gathered at scale. And formal channels exist, like youth advisory groups and youth parliaments. Three haven't. Visibility still isn't impact, just as counting posters wasn't. Someone still has to decide, so someone still has to be asked. And sustained pressure still beats a moment.

Formal channels bring a risk, tokenism: involving young people visibly, while giving them no influence. Picture a ladder of participation. Young people can be informed, consulted, partners, or leaders. Consultation is where tokenism hides. The test is simple. Can you name a decision that was made differently because of what young people said? If they were listened to, thanked, and nothing changed, that was tokenism.

scenes.title: within a community, and audience before mode

voiceover.text: Finally, the syllabus asks about individuals within their communities, and within is the key word. Advocacy has a range of reach. Self-advocacy, then speaking up for one other person, then acting through a structure that already exists, like a student council, club or cultural organisation, then an organised campaign, and finally policy. Existing structures come with an audience, a relationship with decision-makers, and they carry on after you leave. Then choose the audience first, and the mode second. A principal wants a short costed proposal. A formal inquiry wants a submission. The public wants one clear story.
Two things to remember. Advocacy needs an ask, and someone who can say yes. And choose the audience first, then the mode.

Two exam questions. First. Students post a video about the unlit basketball courts at their local park. It's viewed forty thousand times, but nothing changes. Explain why, and outline what the students should do next. Pause here to answer.

It changed nothing because visibility isn't impact. There was no specific ask, and no decision-maker who had to answer. Next, they should write a short proposal to the council, which runs the park, asking for lights on the courts until eight on weeknights, with a cost, a date, and evidence from the players affected. The classic mistake is thinking more views would have done it.
Second. Examine how young people have advocated for their own and others' health, referring to past and current advocacy. Pause here to answer.

Define advocacy against education and awareness, with an ask and an audience. Then a past case, like the nineteen sixty-five bus tour, linked to the determinants it targeted. Then current advocacy, and compare: cheap reach and formal channels have changed, but visibility still isn't impact, and pressure must last. End on individuals acting within community structures. The classic mistake is a list of campaigns with no comparison.

So, find the decision-maker, make a specific ask, check sources of different kinds, and choose the mode for the audience. Next, young people aren't the only advocates. What do governments, organisations and communities each do?
